cards.title: Hexagonal Architecture — Cockburn's Big Idea
cards.teaser: In 2005, Alistair Cockburn published 'Hexagonal Architecture' to solve one persistent problem: application logic entangled with delivery mechanisms and infrastructure, making the core impossible to test or reuse.

runs.text: Before hexagonal architecture, the dominant structure was a layered stack: Presentation on top, Business Logic in the middle, Data Access at the bottom. This worked until it didn't. Business logic sprouted database annotations. Services imported HTTP request objects. Test suites required a running web server and a live database to exercise a single if-statement.
Alistair Cockburn's 2005 paper,
Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)

, proposed a different mental model. The application has an inside and an outside. The inside — the domain and its use cases — is pure logic. The outside is everything the application talks to: users, databases, message queues, external APIs. The boundary between inside and outside is enforced by explicit, named interfaces.

Cockburn called his diagram a hexagon not because six sides are significant, but because a six-sided shape conveniently shows multiple entry points around the perimeter without implying a top-down hierarchy. Any side of the hexagon can host a port. The shape deliberately breaks the top-is-input, bottom-is-database assumption of the layered diagram.

Cockburn's original paper is freely available at alistair.cockburn.us/hexagonal-architecture. It is short — roughly 3,000 words — and worth reading in full. Much of what circulates as 'hex arch guidance' is a distillation of that single document.

Hexagonal architecture says: put your business logic in the center, surrounded by a wall of interfaces. Everything outside — the web framework, the database, the email sender — connects through those interfaces, not directly to the logic.

cards.title: Ports and Adapters — The Naming Pair
cards.teaser: A port is an interface — a named contract declaring what the application needs or offers. An adapter is an implementation of that interface for a specific technology. Ports live inside; adapters live outside.

runs.text: The pattern is named
Ports and Adapters

— 'Hexagonal Architecture' is the nickname Cockburn gave to the resulting diagram. Understanding both terms precisely prevents a common mistake: treating them as interchangeable or conflating the interface with its implementation.

items.text: — a named interface on the boundary of the application. It defines a contract in the application's own language, without reference to any technology. A port might be named
. It knows nothing about SQL, HTTP, or Stripe.
— a concrete class that implements a port using a specific technology. A
port. Adapters depend on the port definition; the application core depends only on the port.

runs.text: The port is the seam. It is the point at which the application's internal world ends and external technology begins. By defining explicit seams, the architecture makes it possible to swap one adapter for another without touching the application core.

This is not an exotic pattern. It is the Dependency Inversion Principle applied at the architectural scale: depend on abstractions, not concretions. Ports are the abstractions. Adapters are the concretions.

A port is the interface your app defines — what it needs or offers, in its own vocabulary. An adapter is a plug that connects a real technology (a database, an HTTP server, an email provider) to that interface. Swap adapters freely; never touch the port.

cards.title: The Hexagon Diagram — A Visual Reference
cards.teaser: The hexagonal diagram makes the port topology visible: primary ports on the left (drivers), secondary ports on the right (driven). The domain sits at the center, unreachable by any outside concern.

runs.text: The canonical arrangement of a hexagonal architecture looks like this:

explanation.code:
[ HTTP Adapter ]   [ CLI Adapter ]
                        |                  |
                  (PlaceOrderPort)   (QueryOrderPort)
                        |                  |
         +--------------------------------------------+
         |                                            |
         |          APPLICATION CORE                  |
         |                                            |
         |   Domain Model + Use Case Orchestration    |
         |                                            |
         +--------------------------------------------+
                        |                  |
               (OrderRepository)  (NotificationPort)
                        |                  |
              [ Postgres Adapter ] [ Email Adapter ]

runs.text: The adapters above the hexagon are
driving adapters
(or primary adapters): they initiate interaction with the application. The adapters below are
driven adapters
(or secondary adapters): they are called by the application.
Every arrow from outside the hexagon points
inward
— toward an interface defined by the application. No arrow from inside the hexagon points outward toward a concrete technology. This constraint is what makes the core portable and testable.
In practice, teams often draw ports and adapters on a flat left-right axis rather than around a hexagon. The shape is incidental; the constraint — all dependencies point inward — is the substance.

Draw a hexagon. Put your domain logic inside. On the left, draw the things that call your app (HTTP, CLI). On the right, draw the things your app calls (database, email). Each connection goes through an interface defined by the center — never a direct wire to a technology.

cards.title: Primary (Driving) Ports — What the Application Offers
cards.teaser: A primary port is a use-case interface that driving adapters call to trigger application behavior. The HTTP controller, the CLI command, and the gRPC handler are all adapters; the use-case interface is the port they call.

runs.text: A
primary port
(also called an inbound port or driving port) is an interface that exposes what the application can do. It represents a use case in the domain's vocabulary:

The controller knows about HTTP. It knows nothing about the domain. The use case interface knows about the domain. It knows nothing about HTTP. This is the fundamental separation the primary port enforces.
Driving adapters that can target the same primary port:

items.text: A message consumer (e.g., a Kafka listener that receives a command event)
A test class in a unit test

runs.text: All five can call
placeOrder()
without changing the application core. The use case implementation is identical regardless of which adapter initiates the call.

A primary port is the application's front door — it's the interface that defines what your app can do, in your domain's language. HTTP controllers, CLI commands, and test code all knock on that door; they don't talk to the internals directly.

cards.title: Secondary (Driven) Ports — What the Application Needs
cards.teaser: A secondary port is an interface the application defines to declare a dependency it needs satisfied from outside — persistence, messaging, email. The application core calls the port; an adapter wires in the technology.

runs.text: A
secondary port
(also called an outbound port or driven port) is an interface defined in the application layer that expresses what the application needs from the outside world — without naming the technology.
The application core imports
OrderRepository
. It never imports
PostgresOrderRepository
. The concrete adapter is wired in at startup time — typically via dependency injection.
Common secondary ports in a DDD application:

items.text: — publishing domain events to a message broker
— abstracting system time (makes time-sensitive logic deterministically testable)

runs.text: A secondary port is the application saying 'I need something from outside — here is the interface it must satisfy.' The app core calls the interface; it never calls PostgreSQL, Kafka, or SendGrid directly. Those are adapters that satisfy the interface.

cards.title: The Dependency Inversion Principle at Architecture Scale
cards.teaser: Hexagonal architecture applies DIP system-wide: the domain defines what it needs; the infrastructure provides it. High-level policy never depends on low-level detail. The interfaces always belong to the domain, not to the adapter.

runs.text: Robert C. Martin's
Dependency Inversion Principle
(DIP) states:

items.text: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.
Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

runs.text: In hexagonal architecture, the domain is the high-level module. The database adapter is the low-level module. Without DIP, the service would import the repository class directly, coupling domain logic to PostgreSQL. With DIP, the domain defines the
OrderRepository
interface, and
PostgresOrderRepository
implements it. The domain owns the abstraction; the infrastructure provides the detail.
The key implication: ports belong to the same package or module as the application core — never to the infrastructure module. If
OrderRepository
lives in the
infrastructure
package, the domain is forced to depend on infrastructure to compile — exactly the coupling DIP is meant to prevent.

A common mistake: placing the repository interface in an 'infrastructure.ports' package. This inverts the inversion. The port must live in 'domain' or 'application', so that the infrastructure layer is the one that carries the dependency, not the domain.

Dependency inversion means the domain writes the contract and infrastructure fulfills it — not the other way around. The interface lives with the domain code; the PostgreSQL adapter reaches out to implement it. Dependency flows toward the domain, never away.

cards.title: The Dependency Rule — All Arrows Point Inward
cards.teaser: The dependency rule is the single constraint that makes hexagonal architecture work: source-code dependencies may only point inward, toward the domain. No domain class may import a class from an outer layer.

runs.text: The
dependency rule
is simple to state:
nothing in the inner ring may know about anything in the outer ring
. This means:

items.text: Domain entities do not import framework annotations (
Domain services do not import HTTP request or response types.
Use case interactors do not import database driver classes.

runs.text: This rule can be mechanically enforced. In Java, ArchUnit allows writing an architecture test:

When the dependency rule is violated, the violation is measurable: the build breaks. Architecture constraints that live only in documentation erode immediately; constraints enforced by tooling erode slowly or not at all.

The dependency rule has one sentence: nothing on the inside may import something on the outside. Domain code never mentions Spring, Hibernate, or Kafka. If you can enforce this in your build tool, violations become compile errors, not review comments.

cards.title: Onion Architecture — Jeffrey Palermo's Concentric Variant
cards.teaser: Jeffrey Palermo introduced Onion Architecture in 2008 as an elaboration of hexagonal architecture: explicit concentric rings — Domain Model, Domain Services, Application Services, Infrastructure — each ring depending only on rings closer to the center.

runs.text: Jeffrey Palermo published Onion Architecture on his blog (jeffreypalermo.com) in 2008, shortly after Cockburn's hexagonal architecture paper. Where Cockburn described two zones — inside and outside — Palermo named four concentric rings:

items.text: (innermost) — entities, value objects, domain events. No dependencies on anything.
— operations that span multiple aggregates. Depends on Domain Model only.
— use case orchestration, transaction coordination. Depends on Domain rings.
(outermost) — adapters for persistence, messaging, HTTP. Implements interfaces defined in the inner rings.

runs.text: Palermo's explicit contribution was naming the rings. Cockburn's hexagon did not distinguish between domain model and application services. Onion architecture provides that granularity, which matters when the domain grows large enough that the application service / domain model boundary becomes load-bearing.

The name 'Onion Architecture' comes from the rings: slice through the architecture and you see concentric layers, like an onion cross-section. The dependency rule is the same as hexagonal: all imports point toward the center.

Onion architecture takes hexagonal architecture and names the layers explicitly: domain model is the core, domain services wrap it, application services wrap those, and infrastructure is the outermost shell. Every layer only imports from layers inside it.

cards.title: Clean Architecture — Uncle Bob's Four-Ring Diagram
cards.teaser: Robert C. Martin's Clean Architecture (2017) extends the same idea with four named rings and universal vocabulary: Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks & Drivers. The dependency rule remains: source-code dependencies point inward.

runs.text: Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob) published
Clean Architecture: A Craftsman's Guide to Software Structure and Design
in 2017, synthesizing hexagonal, onion, and several other layered approaches into a single model with precise names:

items.text: (innermost) — enterprise-wide business rules. Domain objects that would exist even if the application did not. In a DDD system: aggregates, entities, and value objects.
— application-specific business rules. The interactors that orchestrate entities to fulfill a single use case. They define the input and output port interfaces.
— controllers, presenters, gateways. Convert data between the format of use cases and the format required by external agencies (frameworks, databases).
(outermost) — Spring, Hibernate, React, PostgreSQL. Details. Nothing in an inner ring may mention a class from this ring.

runs.text: Martin's clean architecture diagram features a prominent arrow labeled 'DEPENDENCY RULE' pointing inward, and the famous note:
"The name of something declared in an outer circle must not be mentioned by the code in an inner circle."

The practical difference between clean architecture and onion architecture is primarily in vocabulary and framing, not in structure. Both extend Cockburn's original insight. In a DDD application, 'Entities' maps to the Domain Model ring and 'Use Cases' maps to Application Services.

Clean architecture is hexagonal architecture with four named rings: Entities (pure domain), Use Cases (orchestration), Interface Adapters (controllers and gateways), and Frameworks (the actual database and web server). The rule is unchanged: nothing from an outer ring gets named in an inner ring.

cards.title: Domain in the Center — Pure, Frameworkless, Fully Testable
cards.teaser: The domain at the core of a hexagonal application has zero framework dependencies. It contains only business logic, expressed in the ubiquitous language. It compiles and tests without a running database, HTTP server, or message broker.

runs.text: The most visible consequence of the dependency rule is what the domain
does not contain
What the domain does contain: aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, domain services, and the port interfaces the application layer needs.
A frameworkless domain is the precondition for full testability. A test for
Order.confirm()
is a plain JUnit test with no Spring context, no database, no test container — just an object instantiated with
new

If you can run your domain model tests with a plain 'java test' command — no Spring context, no database, no web server — your domain is in the center. The moment a domain class imports a framework annotation, the domain has leaked outward.

cards.title: The Application Layer — Orchestrating Use Cases
cards.teaser: The application layer sits just outside the domain. It implements primary ports (use cases), coordinates domain objects, manages transactions, and calls secondary ports. It contains no business rules and no framework dependencies.

runs.text: The
application layer
(called 'Use Cases' in clean architecture and 'Application Services' in onion architecture) is responsible for:

items.text: Implementing the primary port interfaces (use cases).
Calling domain methods to execute business rules.
Publishing domain events via secondary ports.

runs.text: Notice what is absent: no
if/else
expressing business rules (those live in
Order.confirm()
), no SQL, no HTTP. The application service is a thin orchestration layer — the thinner the better.

The application layer is the conductor: it loads the domain objects, tells them to do something, saves the results, and fires the events. It makes no business decisions itself — those belong to the domain. It uses no infrastructure directly — those are called through secondary ports.

cards.title: Infrastructure Adapters — The Technology Layer
cards.teaser: Infrastructure adapters implement secondary ports using real technology: a JPA repository, a Kafka producer, a SendGrid email client. They are interchangeable by design — swapping one adapter never touches the domain or application layer.

runs.text: The infrastructure layer is the outermost ring. It contains all the technology-specific code that the domain and application layers expressly forbid. An infrastructure module typically contains:

items.text: — JPA entity classes, JdbcTemplate queries, MongoDB document mappers. These implement repository ports defined in the application layer.
— Kafka producers and consumers, RabbitMQ publishers. These implement
— RestTemplate or WebClient calls to external services. These implement payment gateway or external catalogue ports.
— SendGrid, Twilio integrations. These implement notification ports.
— Spring MVC controllers, gRPC service implementations, Kafka message consumers. These call primary ports.

runs.text: A key structural discipline: infrastructure adapters often need a
mapping step
between the domain model and the persistence model. The
Order
aggregate should not inherit from a JPA
@Entity
base class. Instead,
PostgresOrderRepository
maps between a
OrderJpaEntity
(persistence model) and the
Order
aggregate (domain model). The mapping is boilerplate, but it is the price of keeping the domain clean.

Infrastructure adapters are where the wires plug in. They know about PostgreSQL, Kafka, and SendGrid. They translate between the domain's clean model and whatever format the outside technology requires. Swap adapters freely; the domain never notices.

cards.title: Testing Benefits — Port Stubs and Real Adapters
cards.teaser: Hexagonal architecture makes testing straightforward: unit tests replace secondary adapters with in-memory stubs; integration tests wire in the real adapters. No framework context is needed to test domain logic.

runs.text: The dependency rule has a direct testing payoff. Because the domain and application layers depend only on port interfaces, tests can supply any implementation:
This test runs in milliseconds. It tests the full application flow — command in, repository saved, event published — without any framework startup or I/O.
For
integration tests
, wire in the real adapters —
PostgresOrderRepository
with a Testcontainers database — and exercise the same use case. The application code under test is identical in both cases. Only the wired adapter changes.

A full testing strategy for a hexagonal application: unit tests (in-memory stubs) for use case logic; adapter tests (one per adapter) for the persistence and messaging implementations; end-to-end tests (full wiring) for a small set of critical paths. The layers map directly onto the test pyramid.

Because your app only talks to interfaces, a test can plug in a fake HashMap instead of PostgreSQL. The test runs in milliseconds and covers the full use case. When you want to verify the real database works, swap in the real adapter — the application code is unchanged.

cards.title: Hexagonal Architecture vs Layered Architecture
cards.teaser: The classical three-tier stack (Presentation, Business Logic, Data Access) and hexagonal architecture look similar on the surface. The critical difference is the direction of the database dependency — and that difference changes everything about testability and evolution.

runs.text: In a traditional layered architecture, dependencies flow downward:

explanation.code:
[ Presentation Layer ]  (imports Business Logic)
           |
  [ Business Logic ]       (imports Data Access)
           |
  [ Data Access Layer ]    (imports ORM / JDBC)

runs.text: The business logic layer imports the data access layer. This means the business logic has a compile-time dependency on the ORM or database driver. Test the business logic and you must wire in a database.
In hexagonal architecture, the domain defines the
OrderRepository
interface. The data access module implements it. The dependency arrow is reversed:

explanation.code:
[ HTTP Adapter ]   ----calls---->  (PlaceOrderPort)
                                           |
                                    [ Application Core ]
                                           |
                                    (OrderRepository)
                                           ^
                                           |
  [ Postgres Adapter ] ----implements---- +

runs.text: What stays the same between the two styles:

items.text: There is still a separation between presentation, business logic, and data access.
There is still a concept of 'services' that orchestrate domain objects.
There are still repository classes that interact with the database.

runs.text: What changes:

items.text: The dependency between business logic and data access is inverted — the interface lives with the domain, not with the data access layer.
The business logic is fully testable without a database or web server.
Delivery mechanisms (HTTP, gRPC, CLI) are interchangeable because they call a port, not the service directly.
The database can be swapped (PostgreSQL to DynamoDB) without touching the domain or application layer.

runs.text: In a layered architecture, the service imports the repository class. In hexagonal architecture, the service imports a repository interface, and the repository class implements it. One arrow is flipped. That one arrow means you can test your entire business logic with no database.

cards.title: Package Structure — Mapping the Architecture to Code
cards.teaser: Hexagonal architecture only delivers its benefits when the package structure enforces the rings. A canonical layout separates domain, application, and infrastructure into distinct packages with explicit, checkable dependency rules.

runs.text: The architecture rings should be visible in the code layout. A canonical package structure for a Java hexagonal application:

explanation.code:
src/main/java/com/example/ordering/
  domain/
    model/
      Order.java
      OrderId.java
      OrderLine.java
      OrderStatus.java
    events/
      OrderPlaced.java
    ports/
      OrderRepository.java        <- secondary port (interface)
      EventPublisher.java         <- secondary port (interface)
  application/
    ports/
      PlaceOrderUseCase.java      <- primary port (interface)
      GetOrderUseCase.java        <- primary port (interface)
    services/
      PlaceOrderService.java      <- implements PlaceOrderUseCase
      GetOrderService.java
  infrastructure/
    persistence/
      OrderJpaEntity.java
      PostgresOrderRepository.java  <- implements OrderRepository
    messaging/
      KafkaEventPublisher.java      <- implements EventPublisher
    web/
      PlaceOrderController.java     <- driving adapter
      OrderRestMapper.java

runs.text: Key discipline checkpoints for this layout:

items.text: Port interfaces (both primary and secondary) are owned by

runs.text: In multi-module Maven or Gradle builds, these packages can be enforced as separate modules with explicit dependency declarations. The build tool then makes illegal dependencies fail at compile time — no test required.

A hexagonal architecture is only as real as its package boundaries. If domain, application, and infrastructure sit in separate packages (or better, separate modules), the compiler enforces the dependency rule. Structure that can be verified is structure that will survive.

cards.title: When to Apply Hexagonal Architecture
cards.teaser: Hexagonal architecture adds structure. That structure pays dividends in complex domains with rich business logic and multiple delivery channels. In simple CRUD services, the overhead may not be warranted — knowing when to apply it is as important as knowing how.

runs.text: Hexagonal architecture is not always the right choice. Like DDD itself, it is a response to a specific kind of complexity. The value grows with:

items.text: If the business rules are complex enough to warrant testing in isolation, the frameworkless domain that hexagonal architecture enables pays off immediately. For a service that is purely a CRUD facade over a database table, the overhead is unwarranted.
If the same use case must be accessible via HTTP, a CLI, and a message queue, primary ports prevent logic duplication across three entry points. A single-channel service sees less benefit.

If the team expects to migrate databases, change message brokers, or adopt a new web framework, secondary ports make those changes cheaper. If the technology stack is stable, this benefit is theoretical.
The investment in adapter separation pays back over years, not months. Short-lived throwaway services do not need it.

runs.text: The decision is not binary. Teams often apply a pragmatic gradient: strict hexagonal architecture for the core bounded contexts that contain the most complex business logic, and simpler layered approaches for utility services and CRUD endpoints.

The most common failure mode of hexagonal architecture in enterprise teams is applying it everywhere uniformly, including to simple CRUD services where it adds ceremony with no benefit. Match the pattern to the problem, not to the organizational style guide.

Hexagonal architecture is investment in structure. It pays off when the domain is complex, there are multiple entry points, or the technology stack will change. Apply it to the parts of your system that need it — not to the CRUD endpoints that are just wrappers over a database table.
